item.title: New Zealand has relaxed the rules for its four-year golden visa – here's what to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Good news: New Zealand's four-year so-called “golden visa” is now open for applications. Travellers from around the world have long been drawn to New Zealand’s diverse wildlife and rich culture. If you’re one of the many who have fallen in love with the island country and entertained the idea of moving there, things just got easier thanks to this new visa – so long as you have spare time and money to invest in a local business. New Zealand officially opened applications for its Business Investor Work Visa on 24 November 2025, allowing eligible foreign investors to live and work in the country for up to four years. Since then the government has relaxed some of the rules, expanding the types of businesses investors can purchase and making it easier to access the scheme. But its greatest benefit is in the fine print: the programme offers a pathway to residency for those willing to invest in and actively run a New Zealand business. Here’s how it works. Applicants can either invest NZ $1 million (£418,000) for a three-year work-to-residency track or NZ$2 million (£836,000) for an expedited one-year path. That’s on top of a visa application fee starting at NZ$12,380 (£5,175) and the requirement of helping run the business in which you invest. After the designated time has passed, visa-holders can then apply to stay in the country indefinitely, via the Business Investor Resident Visa. However, those choosing the fast-track option must still operate their business for at least three years in total, even if they become eligible for residency after just 12 months. There are some further stipulations: applicants must have funds of at least NZ$500,000 (£209,000) to cover their own and their family’s needs (they can bring their partner and dependent children), and must demonstrate three years’ experience actively managing and operating a business full-time; this might include having at least five full-time employees or earning an annual revenue for your business of at least NZ$1 million (£418,000). Applicants must also be aged 55 or under and meet English-language requirements. Expect limitations around the companies you can invest in too. For example, they must be at least five years old. And some industries are barred, including gambling enterprises, fast-food outlets and businesses involved in manufacturing tobacco or nicotine products. Eligible businesses must also employ at least five full-time-equivalent staff; investors must acquire at least a 25% stake and create one additional full-time job for a New Zealand citizen or resident. The scheme has also become more flexible. On 6 July 2026 the government began to relax the rules, allowing applicants to invest in eligible franchise businesses, purchase companies through New Zealand resident entities and use gifted funds, provided they were lawfully earned. The changes are intended to make the visa more accessible and encourage further investment in the country's businesses. How does it compare to other New Zealand visas? This isn’t New Zealand’s first residency-by-investment rodeo. The country already has an Active Investor Plus golden visa programme, although it does have higher investment requirements: NZ $5 million (£2.09 million) in the Growth category, which requires investors to maintain their investment for three years, or NZ$10 million (£4.18 million) in the Balanced category, which offers a wider range of investment options over five years – on top of an application fee of NZ$27,470 (£11,480). In return investors and their families can obtain a resident visa, allowing them to live, work and study in New Zealand indefinitely, with the possibility of applying for permanent residency after three or five years, depending on the investment category, provided they meet the relevant conditions. Unlike the Business Investor Work Visa, the Active Investor Plus programme does not require applicants to actively manage a business. Interest in the scheme has grown considerably since its requirements were relaxed in April 2025. According to the latest figures from Immigration New Zealand, 1,021 people applied for the scheme between 1 April 2025 and 10 November 2026, with 531 of their applications approved. US citizens accounted for the largest share, submitting 319 applications, followed by applicants from China and Hong Kong. The government reports around NZ$5.5 billion (£2.3bn) in committed investment and investment still in the pipeline, although not all of that money has been invested yet. The Active Investor Plus Visa is considered a useful alternative to the Business Investor Work Visa, especially for those not able to take a proactive role in running a business. For those without millions to invest, there are other ways to spend more time in New Zealand. Since 27 January 2025 people applying for visitor visas have been allowed to work remotely for overseas employers or clients while travelling in the country, provided they meet the relevant visa conditions. This does not extend to working for New Zealand employers or clients. It's not a separate digital nomad visa, but it does offer more flexibility for those hoping to combine work with an extended stay.

item.title: Is there a tube strike today? All the London strike dates to know for 2026 – and how to navigate them
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
London's glittering Christmas transformation is in full swing, with Christmas markets, festive light trails and the West End's most Christmassy productions underway. Travellers trying to get around the London festivities should triple-check their map apps while various train disruptions are hitting the London Underground this weekend. For those planning a visit to the capital in the next few months, there will likely also be another wave of strikes in December, January and February. Here's what to know as you navigate the capital. On Friday 27 November, there'll be disruption expected across several lines, mostly till 12pm. While trains are set to get back to normal after that, you should expect some afternoon business aboard the trains as the lines recover. - Piccadilly and Circle lines: no service expected until after midday - Normal services should be up and running by 6pm - Elizabeth line, London Overground, DLR, buses and trams are expected to operate, although services may be busier than usual This weekend (28 and 29 November) should be all clear of Tube strikes, though you may come across quite a few other disruptions. Avoid travel chaos by planning your alternative journey ahead of time – hop on a bus, give a Lime Bike a go or settle in to watch a Christmas film. Major engineering works this weekend: - Elizabeth line: Most of the line will be down this weekend - Hammersmith & City line: No service this weekend - Circle line: No trains between Hammersmith/High Street Kensington and Tower Hill - District line: No trains between High Street Kensington and Edgware Road - Metropolitan line: No trains between Baker Street and Aldgate - Northern line: No Night Tube between Kennington and Stockwell - Windrush Overground: No service between Highbury & Islington and Battersea Park or Clapham (use the Mildmay line instead) How to get to Heathrow during the Tube strikes Trying to catch a flight today? Travellers can still use the Elizabeth line on Friday 27 November, although there are currently severe delays between Paddington and Heathrow Terminals thanks to engineering works finishing late. The Heathrow Express is also running as normal between Heathrow and London Paddington. Expect delays on the Piccadilly line, though it is still running. When are the next Tube strikes? We have a few weeks set to be strike-free in December, with the next strikes currently planned for just before Christmas, on 17-18 December.
